outline.description: Introduces the problem setting of adapting pretrained text-to-image diffusion models to downstream tasks. This chapter motivates why controllability matters, defines the two target tasks studied in the paper, and frames finetuning as a trade-off between adaptation power and preservation of pretrained generative ability.
subtopics: Overview of modern text-to-image diffusion models and their capabilities
Why text prompts alone are often insufficient for precise image control
Subject-driven generation: generating a specific subject in new contexts from a few reference images
Controllable generation: conditioning on extra signals such as edges, segmentation maps, or landmarks
The core challenge of finetuning without destroying pretrained semantics
Desiderata for finetuning: training efficiency and preservation of generalizable generation
Limitations of naive full finetuning and standard small-learning-rate updates
Why parameter-efficient adaptation methods are attractive for diffusion models
The paper’s central thesis: preserve semantic structure during finetuning through orthogonal transformations

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Background on Diffusion Models, Adaptation, and Related Tasks
outline.description: Builds the conceptual background needed to understand the paper. It reviews text-to-image diffusion models, prior subject-driven and controllable generation methods, and parameter-efficient finetuning approaches such as LoRA and adapters.
subtopics: Brief review of diffusion and latent diffusion models
Stable Diffusion as the pretrained backbone used in the paper
Pixel-space versus latent-space text-to-image diffusion models
Subject-driven generation methods before OFT
DreamBooth and its prior-preservation finetuning framework
Controllable generation methods before OFT
ControlNet and T2I-Adapter as strong controllable generation baselines
Parameter-efficient finetuning in large pretrained models
LoRA: low-rank additive updates and their intuition
How OFT differs from LoRA, adapters, and full finetuning

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Why Semantics May Live in Angles, Not Magnitudes
outline.description: Explains the paper’s key intuition that angular relationships among neurons are central to semantic preservation. This chapter develops the geometric motivation behind OFT and connects it to prior work on hyperspherical representations and angular similarity.
subtopics: Neuron direction versus neuron magnitude in neural representations
Angular similarity as a semantic signal in representation learning
Hyperspherical embeddings and normalized neurons
SphereNet and related evidence that direction can encode essential information
The toy autoencoder experiment from the paper
Inner product, magnitude-only, and angle-only feature map generation
Empirical finding: angular information nearly preserves image semantics while magnitude does not
The analogy to Fourier phase and magnitude
Why changing neuron directions is a natural way to change generated image semantics
The risk of unconstrained directional changes during finetuning

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Hyperspherical Energy as a Structural Preservation Principle
outline.description: Introduces hyperspherical energy as the paper’s structural measure of semantic preservation. The chapter explains what hyperspherical energy measures, why it is more informative than Euclidean distance alone, and how its invariance motivates orthogonal finetuning.
subtopics: The need for a structural metric beyond Euclidean distance to pretrained weights
Definition of hyperspherical similarity and pairwise angular relationships
Definition of hyperspherical energy for a layer of neurons
Interpreting hyperspherical energy as a measure of neuron uniformity and relational structure
Why preserving pairwise neuron relations may preserve pretrained semantics
Formal expression of hyperspherical energy for normalized neurons
The paper’s finetuning objective: minimizing hyperspherical energy difference from the pretrained model
Why regularizing hyperspherical energy directly is difficult
Invariance of pairwise angular relationships under shared orthogonal transformation
How this invariance leads to a principled finetuning design

outline.description: Presents the main method of the paper. OFT finetunes a layer by applying a learned shared orthogonal matrix to the pretrained weights, thereby preserving hyperspherical energy while still adapting the model to a new task.
subtopics: Conventional finetuning as implicit minimization of deviation from pretrained weights
LoRA as a low-rank additive update constraint
OFT as a multiplicative update that preserves pairwise neuron angles
Fully connected layer notation and forward pass under OFT
Learning a layer-shared orthogonal matrix for each finetuned layer
Rotation and reflection as semantic-preserving transformations on neuron sets
Proof intuition: orthogonal transformations preserve pairwise angles and hyperspherical energy
Identity initialization so finetuning starts exactly from the pretrained model
Why OFT can be interpreted as changing the coordinate system of neurons
The role of orthogonality as a regularizer balancing flexibility and stability

outline.description: Focuses on how to implement OFT efficiently in practice. It explains why generic orthogonalization is too expensive, how Cayley parameterization provides a differentiable alternative, and how block-diagonal structure improves parameter efficiency.
subtopics: Why direct orthogonalization methods such as Gram-Schmidt are costly
Cayley parameterization of orthogonal matrices
Skew-symmetric matrices and the construction R = (I + Q)(I - Q)^(-1)
Orthogonality guarantees under Cayley parameterization
Restriction to determinant 1 and why it is acceptable in practice
Computational and memory costs of full orthogonal matrices
Block-diagonal orthogonal matrices as a parameter-efficient design
Controlling the number of blocks with the hyperparameter r
Complexity reduction from O(d^2) to O(d^2 / r)
Optional block sharing and further reduction to O(d^2 / r^2)
Comparison of OFT and LoRA parameter counts
Concrete example comparing trainable parameter numbers for OFT and LoRA

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 7: Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT) and Re-scaled OFT
outline.description: Introduces the stability-oriented extension COFT and the flexibility-oriented extension re-scaled OFT. This chapter explains why explicit constraints near the pretrained model can help, and how these variants modify the original OFT formulation.
subtopics: Motivation for adding an explicit neighborhood constraint around pretrained weights
COFT forward pass and the deviation constraint ||R - I|| <= epsilon
Interpreting COFT as combining structural preservation with bounded movement
Approximating the Cayley transform near identity using the Neumann series
Moving the deviation constraint from R to Q

Zero initialization of Q for identity initialization of R
How epsilon controls the flexibility-regularity trade-off
Empirical intuition for why COFT improves stability over OFT
Re-scaled OFT: adding a learnable positive diagonal scaling matrix
Why scaling neuron magnitudes does not change hyperspherical energy
Benefits and limitations of adding magnitude flexibility

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 8: Broader Interpretation and Theoretical Insights
outline.description: Synthesizes the paper’s conceptual insights. It explains OFT’s relationship to model architecture, compares OFT to LoRA more deeply, and discusses why OFT may converge faster and preserve generation quality better than competing methods.
subtopics: Architecture-agnostic nature of OFT

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 9: Experimental Design and Evaluation Methodology
outline.description: Describes how the paper evaluates OFT. This chapter covers the backbone model, benchmark tasks, training protocols, fairness considerations, and the metrics used for both subject-driven and controllable generation.

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 12: Practical Lessons, Limitations, and Open Problems
outline.description: Concludes the textbook by distilling the main lessons of the paper, the practical significance of OFT, and the unresolved research questions raised by the authors. It also encourages readers to think critically about future directions for controllable diffusion finetuning.
subtopics: Summary of the paper’s main empirical and conceptual contributions
